TRAVEL VS INVESTMENT - THE NEW MILLENNIAL TREND

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Young Professionals are choosing life experiences & travel over the security of property investments & pension funds – we explore this new generational trend.

Summary:
Millennials have itchy feet - motivated to make money so they can spend it on travel and life experiences rather than tying them down with property bonds and car installments. It’s all about work flexibility and benefits that result in life experience rahter than traditional wealth.

Further information:
Millennials have a bad reputations…. Stereotypes range from - They’re entitled; they’re job-hoppers; they’re the narcissistic selfie generation; they are neither respectful nor patient and they want special privileges.
BUT THEY ARE CHANGING THE WORKING WORLD – MOTIVATED BY TRAVEL AND EXPEIRENCES.

Millennials are not just digital natives, they are the first truly global citizens of the world. They are planet lovers, and great savers for trips. As it turns out, urbanized young people relish diversity, in all of its flavors. National patriotism is less of a stickler value of young people today, as they fiercely value world travel. Global citizens are urbanized, cosmopolitan and free.

Their desire to see faraway places is their main reason to work — after, of course, paying basic necessities – food and shleter. A hefty 70 percent of millennials say their “overwhelming desire to travel” is their main motivation on the job

Millennials are blissfully experiential.
BUT WHY THIS SHIFT?
Millennials are growing up in a world where travel is easier and relatively cheaper than for previous generations and they are taking full advantage of this to travel the globe in search of new experiences.
The current generation of young people differs from their parents’ generation. They have other values.
The point is that people now don’t want prosperity and stability — all they want is flexible schedules and financial and geographical independence.
Millennials are pioneering the sharing economy, the on-demand economy, the gig economy and are more mobile than ever, often changing cities as they change jobs, romantic partners or countries. Millennials are as some put it, programmed to travel. Millennials appear to value experiences more than stuff, more than houses, stability and traditional concerns than GenXers.
PWC RESEARCH – MILLENNIALS ARE RESHAPING THE WORKPLACE
The operate in a different space – where they are not attracted and retained with pension funds and housing subsidies – they want cash and time off – work flexibility and opportunities for personal growth. It changes how employers structure contracts with Millennials – because what worked for Generation X and Baby Boomers – doesn’t work for this generation – if you want to keep the talent – the work environment has to change as well.
WHY NO ROOTS?
A desire to be part of a global world that is more connected and accessible than any other time. Stability – be it here in SA, the States or the East – young professionals are reluctant to be tied down to bonds and property in one country – they want it all and they want to be every where. This generation also has the benefit of parents that are more traditionally stable in their careers and have set down roots building up nest eggs and security that offers their Millennial children a safety net – giving them the confidence to break free and live a more experimental life filled with experiences rather than things.
WHO ARE THESE GLOBAL CITIZENS
They are young professionals – with real jobs – not just waiters and barman – they have tertiary level education, they make money – but they choose to spend it differently.
CASE STUDY 1
Hlangabeza Bhengu is 26. He has a degree in philosophy from UKZN, and is now teaching English in Vietnam – he travels regularly and has been to Thailand, Cambodia and Mongolia. We’ll do a Skype interview.
CASE STUDY 2
Jackie Atsango is 26. She has a degree and worked at Transnet – she’s just quite her job after four years with the company and is heading to Columbia. Last year she went overseas for the first time to Cambodia and realized she wants a life full of experiences. And with her her degree she is willing to take the risk – feeling more free and confident than ever before. Her parents are a little concerned about her travel plans – they are more traditional and would like her to settle down.
CASE STUDY 3
I’m still looking for a third – ideally – someone in SA, who has a good job and travels with savings and leave.
EXPERTS
Gerald Seegers from PWC – worked on the Millennial Research
Andrea Kraushaar from Youth Dynamix - Authority & pioneer in the under 30’s & family space in Africa.

Press Release:


NO PRESS RELEASE ISSUED.
They are millennials. They’re driven by their desire to live their lives in the now, racking up a wealth of experiences rather than traditional wealth & security in the form of assets, property and investments.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: They’re fearless, they’re boldly experimental and explorers at heart.

LINK: They are millennials. They’re driven by their desire to live their lives in the now, racking up a wealth of experiences rather than traditional wealth & security in the form of assets, property and investments.

JACKIE: // Life is too short, the opportunity might not be there.

VO: People born between 1980 and 2000 fall into the Y Generation but are commonly referred to as Millennials – a label many of them resist.

They are well educated and bring in the bucks, but they choose to spend it differently. Splurging 34% of their debit & credit card spend on experiences.

They want to explore the world – living their adventures, rather than just dreaming of them.

Andrea Kraushaar has done extensive research in the under 30’s market in Africa.

ANDREA: Their brains are wired completely differently to a generation prior to them, they act differently they behave differently and yah they are a completely different beast. INT1 M2 //

LINK: Global research shows that close to 70% of millennials are more likely to hop on plane to far-away destinations than putting down a deposit on a property - ranking travel as one of the main motivators to work and earn money after basic necessities like food and shelter.

PORTIA: First of all it is about survival, it’s about shelter, it’s you know looking towards your family looking what they need and but certainly after that travel is certainly one of the items that is on the top of my list.
VO: 26 year-old qualified attorney, Portia Daniell has been to 15 countries on 6 continents. For her, travelling is more than just a holiday.
PORTIA: // I don’t think it’s about taking a break - it’s about learning – a lot of the places I choose to go to – it’s a different culture, it’s about learning how to do things differently on the other side of the world.

VO: Gina Hayden is a conscious leadership specialist based in the UK – she has interviewed Millennials from around the globe.

GINA: They are no longer willing to go sit in the corner office for forty years and wait for their retirement // they want something more immediate to the greater world.

VO: It appears that while some are saving some money, it’s usually not for big purchases.

GINA: What some of the big economic studies are showing // is we are moving from a product economy where we buy things, // to an experience economy.
VO: That’s exactly how 26 year-old Electrical Engineer, Jackie Atsango is spending her hard earned cash.
JACKIE: I spend whatever is left from investing and saving on my experiences, my hobbies and outdoor adventures, I like to go hiking and visit some places, a bit of travelling.
VO: Last year she went overseas for the first time to Myanmar – a trip that has changed her forever.
JACKIE: about Myanmar – how it’s different
VO: Jackie’s generation is seen as the first truly global citizens of the world - urbanized young people that relish diversity, in all of its flavors – they are cosmopolitan and free flowing.
ANDREA: They are very confident as a generation – they have no problem with change and with outer types of people – diversity, cultures

VO: At 26, Hlangabeza Bhengu has a degree in Philosophy and is teaching English in Vietnam. We spoke to him via Skype.

CLAIRE: Described as a fearless generation…
BHENGU: I’m not fearless _ I’m afraid of snakes… (laughs)

VO: Hlangabeza is quite philosophical about it all, pointing out that time is limited and nothing is guaranteed.

BHENGU: // You carrying on with the 2.5 kids, perfect job, perfect wife – and everything is just perfect – life isn’t like that // you having this accumulated wealth isn’t everything – the recession, you’ve seen people lose all their money // experiencing life – you’ll never loose that.

VO: It’s a generation that chooses a less traditional life, opting for a more minimalist one, that will help them fuel their desire to explore and feed their travel fixes.

JACKIE: I don’t have too many responsibilities at the moment – I haven’t bought a house yet and that was an option – do I buy a house or do I something else.

PORTIA: Our focus is trying to achieve a balance life – it’s not you’ll focus on work and then after finish your job go on that cruise // – we want everything at the same time.
VO: With four years experience in the working world – Jackie has just quit her job and is heading to Columbia – she wants a life full of experiences…
JACKIE: I really didn’t see a way to achieve that with 21 days leave or something like that – I chose to leave my job temporarily – go see a new country, learn a new language – live completely differently, letting go of the comforts I have now. INT1 M7
GINA: They are moving from wanting stuff and collecting stuff in the future to wanting something right now that is a meaningful experience – that makes them a better version of themselves or fullfills their values, and their sense of higher purpose – makes them feel relevant in the world. INT3 M2

VO: While they appear to be disconnected from their immediate environments, they are tapped into a bigger world with the understanding that everything and everyone is connected.

GINA: They are the first generation that is born with a human upgrade already in place // They are thinking about questions that maybe hasn’t occurred to us before. How are we responsible in the world – how are we leading consciously, not just doing what’s good for me, but what’s good for everyone – how do we move from me to we?

VO: Born into a digital world that is more accessible than ever before – they are programmed to travel. Going in search of new experiences across the globe on another continent is as natural to them as going to the movies.

ANDREA: With technology, social media, cellphones – it’s like a click of a button, you book a flight, a place to stay via AirBNB, jump into a taxi using Uber on your phone – so it isn’t; a scary space to go navigate it almost opens a whole new world to go and explore….

VO: Using his qualifications to fund his trips, Hlangabeza has a seven year travel plan with places like India, the Maldives and Brazil on his bucket list.

BHENGU: There is so much more life compared to what I lived that side –//I would rather spend my money and enjoy myself than compared to saving up for something in the future.

VO: But not all young professionals are not the same…

LINK: They experience different degrees of wanderlust - in South Africa – having the financial security to buy a home does still hold value.

PORTIA: I am going to put down my roots in the next five years, but right now the value that I see in travelling certainly outweighs the accumulation of assets.

PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: Young Professionals are choosing life experiences & travel over the security of investments and property.

PORTIA: Right now the value that I see in travelling certainly outweighs the accumulation of assets.

VO: We explore this new generational trend.



PROMO 2
VO: Accumulating assets is not a top priority for many young professionals – they’re choosing to explore the world.

JACKIE: Do I buy a house or do I something else. I decided I’d like to see more places.

VO: They’re opting for a wealth of experiences instead.



PROMO3

VO: Millennials are programmed to travel – they have been born into a digital world -.

ANDREA: It almost opens a whole new world to go and explore.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Young Professionals are choosing life experiences & travel over the security of property investments & pension funds – we explore this new generational trend.
metadata.Summary: Millennials have itchy feet - motivated to make money so they can spend it on travel and life experiences rather than tying them down with property bonds and car installments. It’s all about work flexibility and benefits that result in life experience rahter than traditional wealth.
metadata.Further information: Millennials have a bad reputations…. Stereotypes range from - They’re entitled; they’re job-hoppers; they’re the narcissistic selfie generation; they are neither respectful nor patient and they want special privileges. BUT THEY ARE CHANGING THE WORKING WORLD – MOTIVATED BY TRAVEL AND EXPEIRENCES. Millennials are not just digital natives, they are the first truly global citizens of the world. They are planet lovers, and great savers for trips. As it turns out, urbanized young people relish diversity, in all of its flavors. National patriotism is less of a stickler value of young people today, as they fiercely value world travel. Global citizens are urbanized, cosmopolitan and free. Their desire to see faraway places is their main reason to work — after, of course, paying basic necessities – food and shleter. A hefty 70 percent of millennials say their “overwhelming desire to travel” is their main motivation on the job Millennials are blissfully experiential. BUT WHY THIS SHIFT? Millennials are growing up in a world where travel is easier and relatively cheaper than for previous generations and they are taking full advantage of this to travel the globe in search of new experiences. The current generation of young people differs from their parents’ generation. They have other values. The point is that people now don’t want prosperity and stability — all they want is flexible schedules and financial and geographical independence. Millennials are pioneering the sharing economy, the on-demand economy, the gig economy and are more mobile than ever, often changing cities as they change jobs, romantic partners or countries. Millennials are as some put it, programmed to travel. Millennials appear to value experiences more than stuff, more than houses, stability and traditional concerns than GenXers. PWC RESEARCH – MILLENNIALS ARE RESHAPING THE WORKPLACE The operate in a different space – where they are not attracted and retained with pension funds and housing subsidies – they want cash and time off – work flexibility and opportunities for personal growth. It changes how employers structure contracts with Millennials – because what worked for Generation X and Baby Boomers – doesn’t work for this generation – if you want to keep the talent – the work environment has to change as well. WHY NO ROOTS? A desire to be part of a global world that is more connected and accessible than any other time. Stability – be it here in SA, the States or the East – young professionals are reluctant to be tied down to bonds and property in one country – they want it all and they want to be every where. This generation also has the benefit of parents that are more traditionally stable in their careers and have set down roots building up nest eggs and security that offers their Millennial children a safety net – giving them the confidence to break free and live a more experimental life filled with experiences rather than things. WHO ARE THESE GLOBAL CITIZENS They are young professionals – with real jobs – not just waiters and barman – they have tertiary level education, they make money – but they choose to spend it differently. CASE STUDY 1 Hlangabeza Bhengu is 26. He has a degree in philosophy from UKZN, and is now teaching English in Vietnam – he travels regularly and has been to Thailand, Cambodia and Mongolia. We’ll do a Skype interview. CASE STUDY 2 Jackie Atsango is 26. She has a degree and worked at Transnet – she’s just quite her job after four years with the company and is heading to Columbia. Last year she went overseas for the first time to Cambodia and realized she wants a life full of experiences. And with her her degree she is willing to take the risk – feeling more free and confident than ever before. Her parents are a little concerned about her travel plans – they are more traditional and would like her to settle down. CASE STUDY 3 I’m still looking for a third – ideally – someone in SA, who has a good job and travels with savings and leave. EXPERTS Gerald Seegers from PWC – worked on the Millennial Research Andrea Kraushaar from Youth Dynamix - Authority & pioneer in the under 30’s & family space in Africa.
